tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (HttpArena, MDA2AV/HttpArena) with public harness and per-framework Dockerfiles, CPU model in site/data/current.json and nginx built with -O3 -march=native; every TrueAsync and competitor rps figure in the record matches the result JSONs. Not A because the TrueAsync extension comes from a pre-built Docker image whose compiler flags are not published.

corrections.caveats: Beats nginx only on the HTTP/2 baseline profiles at low connection counts and on static-h2; it loses to nginx on baseline-4096 (0.69x), pipelined (0.57x), limited-conn (0.68x), json-h2c (about 0.71x) and json-tls (0.60x), and it trails the C++ agensio (14,744,015 req/s at baseline-h2-256) and C h2o (16,106,978) by roughly 3x on HTTP/2; against C++ proxygen it is 1.03x at baseline-h2c-256 but 0.70x at 1024 and 4096 (derived from page data). Response sizes differ on the baseline profiles: bytes per response derived from the bandwidth column are about 21 for TrueAsync versus about 62 (h2c) and 87 (h2) for nginx, so part of the gap is header bytes; static-h2 is like-for-like (about 15 KB per response for both, 15.88 vs 12.30 GB/s). The HttpArena nginx entry is a custom C handler module (nginx 1.31.4, quictls, worker_processes auto), not stock nginx. The TrueAsync image is a pre-built trueasync/php-true-async:0.7.0-rc.6-php8.6 (the entry's README still names 0.7.0-beta.5), so the extension's build flags are not visible and the tier stays at B. The core is C code (llhttp, nghttp2, libuv), so this is a C library with a PHP front end rather than a PHP-versus-C result; the repo itself publishes no benchmark numbers (only h2load log files).

notes: All claimed figures re-derived from HttpArena result JSONs for true-async-server, nginx, drogon, h2o, agensio and proxygen; license Apache-2.0, 72 stars, last commit 2026-10-06 confirmed. Shortcomings: win limited to HTTP/2 baseline at low connection counts and static-h2, slower than nginx on HTTP/1.1, pipelined and JSON profiles, about 3x behind h2o and agensio on HTTP/2; extension build flags unpublished; not an other-language win since the server core is C.

tier_reason: First-party README table (102,203 vs 49,930 RPS at c=256; 96,143 vs 41,740 at c=512; 100% vs 91.5% HTTP/2 success; +0.82 vs +1.35 ms) with no CPU model, nginx version or config; the repo's benchmark scripts are public but no raw results are published and the shipped backend cannot have produced these numbers.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Arc built with cargo build --release -p arc-gateway (docs/benchmarks/index.mdx); Cargo.toml release profile opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort; nginx build and flags not stated; wrk and h2load used as load generators
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers; the README table gives no nginx version or configuration, no CPU model and no tool flags. The repo ships a reproducible benchmark workflow (benchmark/scripts/run_h1_wrk_vs_nginx.sh, which writes the nginx.conf it uses and records versions in env.txt) but benchmark/results holds only .gitkeep, so no raw runs are published. In that script the backend is benchmark/backends/http_ok_backend.py, a Python ThreadingHTTPServer returning 2 bytes with the default HTTP/1.0 protocol_version, so it closes every upstream connection and neither proxy's upstream keepalive 1024 can take effect; Arc runs with ARC_WORKERS=1 by default while nginx uses worker_processes auto, and wrk runs on the same 2 vCPU host as the servers. A Python backend of that kind is unlikely to sustain the 50k to 100k RPS in the table, so the backend and settings behind the README numbers are probably different and are not stated. The HTTP/2 row compares success rates, not speed. The docs site arc.sdjz.wiki did not resolve (ENOTFOUND); docs/benchmarks/index.mdx in the repo holds methodology only, no results. Tier C: first-party with partial methodology.

notes: README numbers match the record; license Apache-2.0, 8 stars, 11 commits, last commit 2026-03-11 (active) confirmed. Shortcomings: first-party only, no CPU model or nginx version/config, no raw results, published benchmark script uses an HTTP/1.0 Python backend that cannot explain 100k RPS so the README setup is undocumented, HTTP/2 row is a success rate not throughput.

tier_reason: Informal first-party wrk transcript in a 2014 gist: nginx 31,780.82 req/s and the Go rows match the record, but nginx version, configuration and served content, Go version and CPU are all missing; numbers without methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: nginx 31,780.82 req/s (avg latency 7.71 ms). Not like-for-like: Go empty handler with GOMAXPROCS=2 62,314.54 req/s (3.79 ms), about 1.96x (derived from page data). Closest like-for-like row: Go cached file server (yosssi/go-fileserver, in-memory cache, io.Copy) 59,517.07 req/s (5.01 ms), about 1.87x (derived from page data). Other Go file-serving variants are slower than nginx: http.FileServer 16,088.43 req/s and go-fileserver with http.ServeContent 25,581.43 req/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go servers started with GOMAXPROCS=2 go run main.go (Go version not stated); nginx build, version and configuration not shown
corrections.hardware: Not stated; a 'mac:~' shell prompt and a /Users/... directory in the file-server code indicate a Mac; CPU model not given
corrections.caveats: Weak, informal result from 2014 (all nine gist revisions are dated 2014-06-23; the page's 'Last active August 7, 2024' is not a content change). Runs last only 2 seconds, the load generator and servers share one machine (apparently a Mac), and Go and nginx versions, nginx configuration (including worker_processes; the stock nginx.conf sets 1 while Go ran with GOMAXPROCS=2) and the served content are not given. The nginx run and Go sections 2 to 4 all report 'connect 155' socket errors, so only about 245 of the 400 wrk connections were open, while the two go-fileserver runs report connect 0, so effective concurrency differs between rows. Section 2 (empty response) and the first run of section 3 (Hello) show byte-identical output (62,314.54 req/s, same socket errors), which looks like a pasted duplicate. The empty-handler and Hello rows do not serve files, so they are not like-for-like with nginx; of the three file-serving rows two are slower than nginx and the faster one serves from an in-memory cache. A commenter notes sections 5 and 6 show identical code, and another asked for the nginx version and configuration without an answer. Gist has no licence, so the code is reference only. Tier C: numbers without methodology.
corrections.why_faster: Not established by the source: no profile and no nginx configuration. The Go file-server win comes from an in-memory cache (go-fileserver), and the Go runs used GOMAXPROCS=2 against an nginx whose worker count is unknown, so the gap may be configuration rather than language.

notes: Numbers verified on the gist page; dates corrected to the 2014-06-23 revisions (abandoned). Shortcomings: no versions, configs or CPU, 2-second runs on one Mac, unequal effective connection counts (connect 155 errors), duplicated output in two sections, headline 1.96x row is not like-for-like and two of three file-serving rows are slower than nginx; possible worker-count asymmetry. Raw gist (gist.githubusercontent.com) was blocked, so details come from the rendered gist page.
